trials.notes: Correctly chose `WP_HTML_Processor::create_fragment()` for structure-aware fragment parsing. Every called method is documented, and there were no `_doing_it_wrong` records. Uses a single token walk, `get_breadcrumbs()` with the current element excluded, `add_class()`, and `get_updated_html()`. Minor deduction: `next_tag()` would have been a simpler documented opener-only walk, and there is no explicit `paused_at_incomplete_token()` policy.

Same high-adherence pattern as trial 1: correct HTML Processor choice, documented APIs only, structural ancestor detection through breadcrumbs, and byte-preserving output via `get_updated_html()`. The fallback on `get_last_error()` is documented and conservative. Minor deduction for scanning all tokens when tag-only walking would suffice, and for not stating an incomplete-token policy.

Correctly chose the HTML Processor and used only documented methods. The single `next_token()` loop and `get_updated_html()` return path are documented and functional. Main deduction: it manually maintains list nesting state instead of using the documented `get_breadcrumbs()` ancestor stack, which is less idiomatic for current-token containment checks even though it passed the frozen cases and additional malformed-list probes.

failure_analysis: No hidden case failed in any trial; all three passed 7/7. The docs did well at steering subjects to the HTML Processor rather than the Tag Processor: the Tag Processor overview says it has no tree awareness, while the HTML Processor overview and support sections explicitly recommend it for nested structure, breadcrumbs, and containment checks. The `get_updated_html()` documentation also successfully prevented normalization/serialization mistakes for class edits. Near-misses: trials 1 and 2 used a broader `next_token()` loop where `next_tag()` would have been enough; trial 3 reinvented ancestor tracking with an opener/closer counter instead of using breadcrumbs. These were not failures, but they show that the docs make the right tools available without quite making the shortest containment pattern obvious.

doc_gaps.problem: The docs explain that breadcrumbs run down to the current node, but they do not show the common pattern of testing the current element's ancestors while excluding the current element.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a short example showing `array_slice( $processor->get_breadcrumbs(), 0, -1 )` and checking whether any ancestor tag is in a whitelist.

doc_gaps.problem: For class or attribute edits on element openers, candidates may overuse `next_token()` plus `get_token_type()` and `is_tag_closer()` guards.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add guidance that `next_tag()` is the preferred loop for tag-opener mutations, while `next_token()` is for text, closers, serialization rewrites, or subtree scans.

doc_gaps.problem: Manual opener/closer counters are possible, but the docs do not clearly say when breadcrumbs are the safer current-location primitive.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a note: for questions like 'is the current element inside X?', prefer `get_breadcrumbs()` or breadcrumb queries; reserve manual state for aggregate facts not represented by the current breadcrumb stack.

doc_gaps.location: html-processor.md / mutation output and incomplete-input guidance
doc_gaps.problem: Fallback policy for class/attribute mutations is spread across `get_last_error()`, `paused_at_incomplete_token()`, serialization, and recipe sections.
doc_gaps.suggestion: Add a concise mutation checklist: check factory `null`, use `get_updated_html()` after queued edits, fall back on non-null `get_last_error()` when the contract requires safe failure, and check `paused_at_incomplete_token()` only when the caller requires proof of complete source bytes.
